title: WHEN GOD MAKES NO SENSE
paragraphs:
WHEN GOD MAKES NO SENSE
The Astonishing Depth of Isaiah 55:8–9 and the Divine Mind That Rewrites Broken Stories
There are moments in life when faith feels easy.
When prayers are answered.
When doors open.
When healing comes.
When the promotion arrives.
When the diagnosis is clear.
When the relationship survives.
When the future looks bright.
But Isaiah 55:8–9 was not written for those moments.
It was written for the moments that leave us staring into the darkness asking a question most believers are afraid to admit:
“God… what are You doing?”
The mother who buried a child.
The husband whose wife walked away.
The believer who prayed for years and still sees no breakthrough.
The prodigal who cannot understand why God allowed the consequences of their rebellion to become so severe.
The exhausted Christian whose life looks nothing like the promises they imagined.
Isaiah speaks directly into that confusion.
Not with an explanation.
Not with a timeline.
Not with a detailed roadmap.
But with a revelation of who God is.
The passage reads:

"For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts."
(Isaiah 55:8–9)
These words have comforted believers for centuries.
Yet they are often misunderstood.
Many people use this passage as a spiritual way of saying, “God works in mysterious ways.”
While that statement contains truth, Isaiah is saying something far deeper.
To understand it, we must step into the original language and context.
The Hebrew text begins:
כִּי לֹא מַחְשְׁבוֹתַי מַחְשְׁבוֹתֵיכֶם
Ki lo machshevotai machshevoteichem.
Literally:
“For not My thoughts are your thoughts.”
The Hebrew word מַחְשָׁבָה (machashabah) means more than a passing thought.
It refers to plans.
Intentions.
Purposes.
Designs.
Strategic objectives.
God is not merely saying He thinks differently.
He is saying His entire plan operates on a level humanity cannot naturally comprehend.
This becomes even more powerful when we remember the context.
Isaiah 55 is one of the Bible’s greatest invitations to grace.
Only a few verses earlier God declares:

"Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that He may have compassion on him, and to our God, for He will abundantly pardon."
(Isaiah 55:7)
The Hebrew phrase translated "abundantly pardon" is astonishing.
It carries the idea of multiplying forgiveness.
Not rationing mercy.
Not reluctantly forgiving.
Not barely tolerating sinners.
But overwhelming them with grace.
And immediately after making that promise, God says:
“My thoughts are not your thoughts.”
Why?
Because humans struggle to imagine grace this big.
If we were God, many of us would not forgive.
We would seek revenge.
We would demand repayment.
We would make offenders earn restoration.
But God does something scandalous.
He forgives.
He restores.
He redeems.
He rewrites.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
This is the thread running through all Scripture.
This is the reason our ministry theme remains:
Because the entire Bible is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Moses killed.
Rahab was a prostitute.
David committed adultery and murder.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet God transformed their stories into testimonies.
Not because their sins were small.
But because His thoughts were higher.
His plans were greater.
His mercy was deeper.
His redemption was stronger.
When Isaiah says God's ways are higher than ours, the Hebrew word used is:
דֶּרֶךְ (derekh)
Meaning:
road
journey
path
manner of living
course of action
God's "ways" are not simply His methods.
They are His entire pathway of accomplishing redemption.
And humanity repeatedly misunderstands that pathway.
The disciples certainly did.
They expected a conquering king.
Instead they received a suffering servant.
They expected a throne.
They got a cross.
They expected political victory.
They witnessed crucifixion.
Nothing about Calvary made sense from a human perspective.
Yet what looked like defeat became the greatest victory in history.
The Apostle Paul later explained this mystery.
Writing in Greek, he declared:
μωρία
(mōria)
“Foolishness.”
The message of the cross appeared foolish to the world.
Yet what humanity considered weakness became God's power.
What humanity considered loss became salvation.
What humanity considered death became life.
This is Isaiah 55 fulfilled.
God's thoughts are not ours.
His ways are not ours.
And thank God they are not.
Imagine if God thought like us.
Peter would never have been restored.
The thief on the cross would never have entered paradise.
The prodigal son would never have come home.
And many of us would still be carrying the weight of our worst mistakes.
The truth is uncomfortable.
Most people want God to explain Himself.
But Scripture consistently reveals that God often invites trust before understanding.
Noah built before rain.
Abraham walked before knowing.
Joseph suffered before reigning.
David was anointed before becoming king.
The disciples followed before fully understanding.
Faith has never been the absence of questions.
Faith is trusting God's character when His plans remain hidden.
Perhaps that is why Isaiah uses one of the most breathtaking comparisons in Scripture:
"As the heavens are higher than the earth..."
Ancient people looked upward and saw endless distance.
The stars appeared unreachable.
The heavens represented immeasurable transcendence.
Today modern astronomy reveals something even more astonishing.
The observable universe spans incomprehensible distances beyond human imagination.
And Isaiah says the difference between God's understanding and ours is greater still.
Not slightly higher.
Not marginally better.
Infinitely greater.
The implications are life-changing.
That closed door may have protected you.
That delay may have preserved you.
That heartbreak may have redirected you.
That season of waiting may be preparing you.
That unanswered prayer may not be divine neglect.
It may be divine wisdom.
The Christian faith does not claim that every tragedy is immediately understandable.
Scripture never minimizes pain.
Jesus Himself wept.
But Christianity does proclaim something extraordinary:
God sees what we cannot.
God knows what we do not.
God is accomplishing what we cannot yet perceive.
And nowhere is this more visible than at the cross.
Humanity saw humiliation.
God saw redemption.
Humanity saw an ending.
God saw a beginning.
Humanity saw scandal.
God saw grace.
That pattern continues today.
Many readers carrying hidden wounds need to hear this:
Your story is not finished.
The chapter you are living in is not the final chapter.
The God who transformed Peter can transform you.
The God who restored David can restore you.
The God who forgave Paul can forgive you.
The God who raised Jesus from the dead can resurrect what appears hopeless.
Isaiah 55:8–9 is not merely about mystery.
It is about mercy.
It is not merely about transcendence.
It is about redemption.
It is not merely about how different God is.
It is about how much better His plans are than ours.
That truth becomes deeply personal when we stop asking, “Why doesn't God think like me?”
And begin thanking Him that He does not.
Because if God's thoughts were our thoughts, many of us would have been discarded long ago.
Instead, we were pursued.
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Adopted.
Transformed.
The Gospel itself is proof that God's thoughts are higher.
No human mind would have designed salvation this way.
A holy God entering human history.
A sinless Savior carrying the sins of sinners.
A cross becoming a throne.
A grave becoming a doorway.
A scandal becoming grace.
Yet that is exactly what happened.
And that is exactly what Jesus still does.
He rewrites stories.
He restores failures.
He redeems brokenness.
He transforms endings.
He turns scars into testimonies.
He turns rebels into sons and daughters.
He turns scandals into grace.
You never know who may be one article away from surrendering their life to Him.
Your testimony may encourage someone else who is struggling to trust Him.
And perhaps the greatest comfort hidden inside Isaiah's words is this:
The God whose thoughts are beyond your understanding is also the God whose love was proven beyond all doubt at Calvary.
The hands that hold the universe are the same hands that bore the nails.
When you cannot understand His plan, remember His heart.
